summary: For ages 13–14, explore evidence-supported explanations linking sustained Large Igneous Province volcanism with mass extinctions. Distinguish long-term CO2-driven warming and ocean acidification, with associated oxygen stress, from short-lived cooling caused by sulphate aerosols following some eruptions. Relate the Siberian Traps to the end-Permian extinction, and examine possible Deccan contributions alongside the major Chicxulub impact at the end-Cretaceous without treating their relative roles as settled or equal. Use an optional model to explore its assumed causal links, an evidence discussion, a diagnostic explanation and a reference timeline; no simulation output independently proves real-world causation. Hydrothermal vents as a possible setting for life’s origin remain a hypothesis.
misconceptions: 'The lava/ash physically killed everything.' — The mass killing was chemical and climatic (CO2-driven warming, ocean acidification, anoxia) over long timescales, not direct incineration by lava.

'Volcanoes cause mass extinction by cooling the planet (volcanic winter).' — LIPs kill mainly by long-term WARMING and acidification; brief aerosol cooling is the supervolcano effect — different mechanism, opposite thermal sign and timescale.
'A LIP is one giant eruption.' — It is sustained flood-basalt volcanism over hundreds of thousands to millions of years; the cumulative gas release, not a single blast, drives the crisis.
'The dinosaurs died purely from the asteroid' (or 'purely from volcanoes').' — The end-Cretaceous is a debated multi-factor event; Deccan volcanism and the Chicxulub impact likely both contributed.
'Ocean acidification just means the sea is poisonous.' — It means falling pH from dissolved CO2 (carbonic acid) that dissolves carbonate shells and reefs, undermining marine food webs.
'Volcanoes are only destructive.' — The same volcanism is also creative: it built atmosphere, land and soils, and hydrothermal vents may be where life itself began.

activities.title: Run the LIP: drive the deep-time extinction chain
steps: Use an optional simplified model of sustained, pulsed flood-basalt volcanism across a large region, rather than a single explosive volcano. Advance a deep-time timeline across hundreds of thousands of years and state that these are modelled processes.

Inspect linked model traces for atmospheric CO2, temperature, ocean pH, oxygen stress and biodiversity. Identify which relationships and timings the model assumes, and distinguish these traces from measured geological data.

Compare the model with and without volcanic CO2 emissions while holding its other inputs fixed. Describe the resulting change within the model, then ask which independent geological evidence supports its assumptions. Do not call the simulated contrast a new empirical test of the ancient extinction.

Compare a schematic short-lived aerosol-cooling pulse with a schematic long-term CO2-warming response, using axes and time scales that keep both readable. Explain that an eruption can emit both CO2 and SO2, and its net effects depend on quantities, timing and atmospheric processes.
Load the Siberian Traps preset beneath the end-Permian 'Great Dying' and the Deccan Traps preset beneath the end-Cretaceous, reading dates off a deep-time line.

In an end-Cretaceous scenario, compare the model’s assumed Deccan-only, impact-only and combined inputs. Discuss how changing the assumptions affects the output, and weigh geological evidence rather than using the model to declare how much each cause contributed.

Consider a separate hydrothermal-vent origin-of-life hypothesis. Explain that early-Earth vent settings are not the same event as the later extinction-producing LIPs, and that the proposed origin setting is not established fact.
activities.insight: Volcanic gases can affect climate and ocean chemistry far beyond local lava flows. CO2 can drive long-term warming and acidification; SO2-derived aerosols can cause shorter cooling, while warming and circulation changes can contribute to oxygen stress. Explain the proposed links using evidence and distinguish a model’s conditional outcome from proof of the ancient causal history.

activities.title: Make ocean acidification mechanistic
steps: Trace how dissolved CO2 participates in reactions that lower seawater pH and reduce carbonate availability. Discuss how this can make calcification harder and, under sufficiently corrosive conditions, cause carbonate structures to dissolve.
Explain in writing why falling pH undermines marine food webs rather than simply making the sea 'poisonous'.
Connect this chain to a modern analogue (present-day ocean acidification from rising CO2) to make the deep-time process concrete.

Annotate a schematic linking added dissolved CO2, lower pH and reduced carbonate availability to stress on calcifying organisms; distinguish possible dissolution under corrosive conditions from an immediate fate for every shell.
activities.insight: Ocean acidification changes carbonate chemistry and can harm calcifying organisms. The effects depend on conditions and species; a lower pH does not mean that every shell or reef immediately dissolves.

activities.title: Diagnostic: how can a Siberian eruption kill life worldwide?
steps: Consider the Siberian Traps around the end-Permian extinction: extensive regional volcanism accompanied a severe global loss of biodiversity, including a very large fraction of marine species, yet lava did not cover the whole planet.
Explain how an eruption in one region could contribute to the loss of most species across the whole planet, including in the oceans.
State explicitly the chain from local lava to global seawater chemistry change.

Using the end-Permian case, explain why a major impact is not required for every mass extinction and why the Siberian Traps are a leading explanation. Distinguish absence of an established impact cause from proof that no impact of any kind occurred.
activities.insight: A regional volcanic episode can contribute to global atmospheric and ocean changes over time; local lava contact cannot explain worldwide marine losses. Link the proposed mechanisms to geological evidence without claiming that the absence of an established impact proves a uniquely isolated cause.

activities.title: In-role scientist debate: asteroid, volcanoes, or both?
steps: Take part in a dialogue with an in-role palaeontologist/geochemist who asks 'was the end-Cretaceous caused by the asteroid, the Deccan Traps, or both?' and presents evidence for each side.

Read supplied evidence about Chicxulub and Deccan volcanism, distinguish the strong case for a major impact contribution from uncertainty over Deccan’s role, and explain which claims the evidence supports or leaves open.

In a second dialogue strand, argue 'volcanoes: destroyer or creator?' — connecting LIPs as killers to hydrothermal vents as a possible cradle of life and to volcanism's constructive role building atmosphere, land and soils.
Justify your position with evidence rather than asserting a single settled answer.
activities.insight: Scientific explanations weigh evidence for mechanisms and timing. The Chicxulub impact has strong support as a major cause of the end-Cretaceous extinction; the role of Deccan volcanism remains a question to assess without assuming equal contributions. Volcanism also creates land and contributes to long-term Earth systems, while a hydrothermal-vent origin of life remains hypothetical.

activities.title: Deep-time reference timeline and discrimination check
steps: Study a deep-time biodiversity curve with the 'big five' extinction drops marked and the Siberian-Traps and Deccan-Traps pulses aligned beneath the end-Permian and end-Cretaceous crashes; tap to reveal annotations on each pulse.

Answer a short set of discrimination questions: for the end-Permian Siberian Traps case, identify the leading proposed long-term kill mechanism (CO2-driven warming, acidification and oxygen stress, not direct lava contact); sequence the proposed LIP→CO2→warming+acidification→extinction chain; and match each LIP to the extinction it overlaps in time, remembering that Deccan's causal contribution to the end-Cretaceous extinction is uncertain and that impact-driven cooling is part of the end-Cretaceous explanation.

Include a discriminator item contrasting a schematic long-term CO2-warming response with a schematic short-lived sulphate-aerosol cooling pulse (noting that any eruption can emit both gases and that net effects depend on conditions), and a multi-factor end-Cretaceous item.

Explain what a shared timeline shows about timing, what a simulation illustrates about its assumed mechanism, and what independent geological evidence would be needed to evaluate a causal explanation. Neither correlation nor model output alone proves the ancient cause.
activities.insight: Learners can place the flagship cases on a shared deep-time axis and reliably discriminate the correct kill mechanism, chain order and cause pairings — while recognising that a correlation display alone does not establish causation.

checkQuestion: The Siberian Traps erupted lava over an area bigger than western Europe around the time of the end-Permian extinction, when about 90% of species died. The lava itself covered only part of Siberia — so how could an eruption in one region kill off most life across the whole planet, including in the oceans?
checkAnswer: The killer was chemistry, not the lava. Over hundreds of thousands to millions of years the eruptions released enormous amounts of CO2 and other gases, driving severe global warming; CO2 dissolving into the sea caused ocean acidification, and warming lowered ocean oxygen. These global chemical and climate changes — not the lava flows themselves — devastated life worldwide, including marine life far from Siberia.
